title: Iron, heavy periods and fibroids
question_forms: Why are my periods so heavy?
Are fibroids more common in Black women?
Should I take iron for heavy periods?
tradition_says: Heavy, painful periods are often treated as something to put up with, and fibroids are widely thought to 'run in Black families'. Iron-rich foods and tonics are commonly used for tiredness.

layer1.plain_answer: Fibroids are very common in Black women and start earlier than in White women. Heavy periods can drain iron, and in a small US pilot most African American women had low iron. Do not treat tiredness or heavy bleeding yourself: ask a doctor for a blood test.

do.text: Note how heavy your periods are, and how tired you feel, and take it to your doctor.
Ask for a full blood count if periods are heavy or you are exhausted.
Ask about iron stores (ferritin) too: low iron was common without anaemia.
Eat iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, pulses and fortified cereals; tea and coffee with meals reduce absorption.

avoid.text: Taking iron tablets without a blood test: the UK's NHS has a doctor recommend them once a test shows low levels.
Assuming a low haemoglobin means the same thing for everyone: laboratory ranges differed by group.

see_someone_when: Periods are so heavy they affect your daily life, last a long time, or you feel exhausted (doctor).
Bleeding between periods or after sex, or pelvic pain (doctor).
A haemoglobin result is flagged low: ask whether iron deficiency or an inherited trait such as alpha-thalassaemia is the cause (doctor).
Fibroids have been seen on a scan and you have symptoms (gynaecologist: removal is one specialist option).

tested.population: 1,364 randomly selected women aged 35-49 in a US urban health plan (Black and White)
tested.design: Ultrasound screening plus records, estimating cumulative incidence of fibroids by age
tested.finding: By age 50, cumulative incidence of fibroids was above 80% for Black women and nearly 70% for White women (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.5-3.4). Fibroids developed at earlier ages in Black women. Fifty-one percent of premenopausal women with no previous diagnosis had ultrasound evidence of fibroids.

source.authors: Baird DD, Dunson DB, Hill MC, Cousins D et al
source.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

tested.population: 1,693 African American women aged 23-35 with no prior fibroid diagnosis
tested.design: Prospective, community-based, ultrasound at enrolment and about 18 months
tested.finding: Among 1,123 fibroid-free women with follow-up, incidence was 9.4% over about 18 months, rising from 6% at ages 23-25 to 13% at 32-35. Women with existing fibroids were more than twice as likely to develop new ones (relative risk 2.3). Average fibroid growth was 89% per 18 months.

source.authors: Baird DD, Patchel SA, Saldana TM, Umbach DM et al
source.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

tested.population: 44 premenopausal African American women, a pilot
tested.finding: Iron deficiency was present in 68.2% and anaemia in 18.2%. Women who reported heavy or very heavy periods had lower haemoglobin, haematocrit and ferritin and more anaemia symptoms. Of those reporting heavy periods, 35% were anaemic. The authors recommend evaluation for iron deficiency and anaemia whenever African American women report heavy bleeding.

source.authors: Bernardi LA, Ghant MS, Andrade C, Recht H et al

tested.design: Analysis of anonymised laboratory data on haemoglobin, MCV, transferrin saturation, ferritin and white cell count
tested.finding: Haemoglobin, haematocrit and MCV were lower in African-Americans. Among all subjects 19.8% of African-American women would be classed as anaemic against 5.3% of White women; after removing iron-deficient and thalassaemic subjects the gap narrowed to 6.1% and 2.77%. The alpha-thalassaemia deletion explained about a third of the haemoglobin difference. The authors say the same reference standards do not apply to all ethnic groups.
tested.note: Laboratory-referred samples, not a population survey. A good example of a measured variable (alpha-thalassaemia deletion) standing behind a race difference.

tested.finding: The NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if heavy periods affect your life or have lasted a while, and says blood tests may check underlying conditions, including iron deficiency anaemia. Fibroids are listed as a cause of heavy periods, and removing them is one specialist option.
tested.note: Page opened 12 Nov 2026 (paraphrase). The NICE NG88 page returned 403, so NICE guidance is not cited.

tested.population: 23,580 premenopausal Black women, Black Women's Health Study
tested.design: Prospective cohort of relaxer use and fibroids (see chemical relaxers entry)
tested.finding: Ever against never relaxer use: incidence rate ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.06-1.30); the authors raise this as a hypothesis.

source.authors: Wise LA, Palmer JR, Reich D, Cozier YC et al

tier_driver: How common fibroids and low iron are in Black women: ultrasound and laboratory studies, not trials.
tier_note: Observational and ultrasound-based data in Black women; no trial tested iron or any self-care for fibroid symptoms in this setting, and the iron-deficiency data are a pilot.
harm_note: No harm signal for the entry's subject in the sources. Untreated heavy bleeding can cause iron deficiency anaemia (Bernardi 2016). Taking iron without a blood test was not studied in what I read.
evidence_summary: Fibroids are very common in Black women: more than 80% had them by age 50 in a US ultrasound study, against nearly 70% in White women, and they start earlier. Heavy periods are linked to low iron, and in a small pilot 68% of African American women had iron deficiency. See a doctor for blood tests rather than treating tiredness or heavy bleeding yourself.
measured_variables: Haemoglobin, MCV, ferritin, transferrin saturation (blood tests)
Alpha-thalassaemia deletion (explains a third of the Hb gap in Beutler 2005)
Self-identified race is the grouping in the fibroid studies; ancestry and other risk factors were not separated in the abstracts
gaps: Untested: whether iron treatment, diet or any home remedy helps heavy periods from fibroids in Black women; reasons for earlier and higher fibroid rates (relaxers are one hypothesis, not proven); vitamin D and fibroids (trials exist, I did not open them). Not verified: UK-specific rates; NICE NG88 content (403). Some do lines (track periods) are general advice, not from these abstracts.
